💡 Key Takeaways
  • With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.
  • For example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home.
  • Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric organization—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.

For example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home. They received quotes for an energy audit ranging from $100 to $200 and asked if this service is actually worth it.

Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric organization—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.

While experts agree that a $50 assessment is less common, even paying a few hundred for one may save you thousands of dollars down the road. That's because it can uncover hidden air leaks that may contribute to higher utility bills and damaging moisture complications.

According to recent reports, “When you seal air leaks, you may prevent water vapor inside your house from turning into liquid inside your walls. This eliminates the need for costly wood rot and mold challenges that may lead to $5,000 or more in repairs and reduces wear and tear on your HVAC unit,” explains Andrew Pho, a home renovation and improvement expert at Mister Balustealing in Toronto.

Energy audits are designed to find what’s causing energy loss in your home, but they’re not all created equal.

Before booking one, confirm what it includes.

“At the very least, it should consist of a blower-door test (a blower fan is set up in a doorway to measure how much air is leaking in or out of the home), check the levels of insulation in your attic, walls, etc., and look at your HVAC system to make sure it’s running efficiently,” says Dennis Vong, founder and owner of Inland Power Wash in Orange County, CA.

Clear, written suggestions on how to improve the energy efficiency of your home are important as well.

“Additionally, you may want to ask if minor fixes like caulking and weatherstripping are included in the audit or available for an additional cost,” Vong explains.

Niki O'Brien, operations manager at Custom Exteriors in Loveland, CO, reinforces the importance of ensuring your home has proper insulation and ventilation in your attic.

“It can prevent dangerous freeze/thaw cycles that can trap moisture and lead to ice damming and interior leaks,” O’Brien says.

If your goal is to improve energy efficiency and reduce the risk of needing repairs, an energy audit is a good idea.

According to Energy Star, proper insulation and air sealing can cut your heating and cooling bills by as much as 15% on average.

“If you spend $200 a month on heating and cooling, that could mean savings of about $30 a month, or $360 a year,” Vong explains.

O’Brien has experienced the benefits of an energy audit firsthand.

“We have seen many cases, including a home we owned personally, that needed additional insulation and resulted in lower energy costs,” says O’Brien.

At the end of the day, the information you get from an energy audit will absolutely save you money in the long run.

“Whether that means getting new, energy-efficient products, adding additional weather proofing to existing systems, or repairing/replacing caulking, insulation, or creating effective ventilation, eventually it will surpass the cost of an audit,” O’Brien adds.

In a recent development, according to the Department of Energy, an energy audit will typically run you between $250 and $600. The good news is you may be able to get one at a subsidized rate.

“I recommend calling your gas and electric providers to see if they offer energy audits at a subsidized rate and what rebates may be available if you were to make any energy improvements to your home,” notes Vong.

Aaron Christy, founder and owner of Indy Roof & Restoration in Indianapolis, notes that in Indianapolis, for example, AES Indiana offers all of its customers a no-cost virtual assessment, and a free in-home assessment if you meet certain income limits.

Your state may also offer a no-cost assessment.

“In my state, Massachusetts, there’s the Mass Save Program, which provides free audits to qualifying homeowners, renters, and landlords,” explains Ted Dow, vice president of delivery at Power Home Remodeling in Boston.

While you’re waiting for an audit, you can perform your own DIY assessment.

Make sure the weatherstripping around your doors and windows isn’t falling apart, check for any dripping faucets or leaking pipes, and make sure your gutters are draining properly away from your foundation.

“Just remember that it’s best to leave the more specialized services to the pros,” adds Vong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:27 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Recent findings suggest that shares of human resources and finance software company Workday Inc. fell more than 7% in late trading today after a softer-than-expected subscription revenue forecast for the current quarter overshadowed fiscal third-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s targets.

For the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, Workday reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.82, up 22% from $2.32 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $2.705 billion, up 11.2% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of $2.75 per share on revenue of $2.69 billion.

In a recent development, subscription revenue rose 12.8% from a year earlier, to $2.532 billion. Net income on an unadjusted basis came to $237 million, down from $252 million in the same quarter a year ago. Included in the quarter were $51 million in restructuring expenses, which followed the manufacturer’s disclosure in late September that it would cut about 2.5% of its workforce, mostly in its product and technology team.

Sources indicate that total subscription revenue backlog grew 6.1%, to $27.548 billion, with the 12-month figure up 12.3%, to $9.216 billion. Free cash flow came to $691 million, up from $550 million. During the quarter, Workday spent $750 million buying back about 3.8 million shares.

Sources indicate that the quarter also saw Workday hold its annual Rising customer conference in Las Vegas in October, when the firm made Sana the new home experience for its platform. Built on technology from Sana Labs AB, which Workday acquired for about $1.1 billion last year, Sana is an AI interface that brings tasks, decisions, meetings and agent activity together in one place. Autopilot Agents, also debuted at the event, are designed to handle routine HR, finance and IT processes in the background.

It has been revealed that on the opening day of Rising, Workday declared that it had agreed to acquire agentic identity platform ConductorOne Inc., better known as C1.ai. That deal closed on Monday. A partnership with Anthropic PBC, also unveiled at Rising, is set to bring Claude together with Sana AI agents and Workday’s HR and finance data.

It has been revealed that “The past few quarters have been our strongest on the innovation and invention front, and in Q3, our AI products drove nearly $150 million in new ACV, more than three times what we delivered a year ago,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Aneel Bhusri, who returned to the top job in February after Carl Eschenbach stepped down. The priority now, Bhusri added, is to get more customers running agents in production.

According to Workday, the number of core customers that have bought at least one of its AI products rose nearly 25% from the previous quarter, to more than 2,200.

Pointing to what he called “ongoing adoption across our AI portfolio,” Chief Financial Officer Zane Rowe remarked the company is raising its full-year targets.

Recent findings suggest that for its fiscal fourth quarter, Workday expects subscription revenue of $2.6 billion, up 10%, and an adjusted operating margin of 31.7%. Full-year subscription revenue is now forecast at $9.958 billion, up 13%, compared with the $9.94 billion to $9.95 billion guided in August. The full-year adjusted operating margin forecast was also raised, to 31.5%, ahead of the 31.1% expected by analysts.

In a recent development, though the full-year numbers moved higher, the fourth-quarter subscription forecast came in narrowly below the $2.61 billion analysts had been expecting. Growth of 10% in the period would also be a step down from the 12.8% Workday posted in the third quarter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A significant part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he remarked.

It has been revealed that but you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

It has been revealed that often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré remarked. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

According to recent reports, and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Recent findings suggest that prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

It has been revealed that this is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

According to recent reports, home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

Sources indicate that however, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” stated Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”.

It has been revealed that there’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” mentioned Zhao.

In a recent development, redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

The biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

In a recent development, on a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

According to recent reports, the biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

According to recent reports, this report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting latest models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

In a recent development, we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company confirmed plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

It has been revealed that its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a tech giant with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

Industry observers note that the UC3 originally released in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t unveiled any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

Sources indicate that I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost matter - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

Microsoft's 24-hour outage had no hacker behind it, and 10 lessons follow for business

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A dormant Windows flaw, not a hacker, caused Microsoft's 24-hour outage.
  • Most corporate risk plans imagine a cloud outage that begins with an intruder, such as a stolen password, a ransomware gang or a hostile state.
  • When a provider of this size fails, whole institutions stop working, not just their email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A dormant Windows flaw, not a hacker, caused Microsoft's 24-hour outage. Here are 10 risk lessons for businesses that rely on one cloud vendor.

Most corporate risk plans imagine a cloud outage that begins with an intruder, such as a stolen password, a ransomware gang or a hostile state. A global Microsoft $MSFT outage began with no intruder at all, and no hacker caused it. Even so, people around the world filed more than 7.4 million reports of trouble during the failure, according to ABC News. A fault inside one company was enough to disrupt work across the globe. The 2024 Microsoft IT outage was linked to CrowdStrike $CRWD, a cybersecurity firm, according to TIME. This time the fault sat inside Microsoft's own systems, in what CBC News reports was the company's second disruption of 2026. For a business, the question is less about who might break in and more about what happens when its provider breaks its own systems.

When a provider of this size fails, whole institutions stop working, not just their email. The Next Web reports that trading firms were delayed and airline communications were disrupted. Finance and air travel usually break down for different reasons, but this time they failed together because they rent the same software, and the weak point sat in a layer that no customer controls.

Recent findings suggest that news18 laid out what went wrong behind Microsoft's "Code Red" and what enterprises should take from it. Its lessons cover a dormant flaw that no hacker planted, the backup channels a firm needs when Teams and Outlook stop working, and continuity prepares built for days rather than minutes. Together, they move the job of staying online from the vendor's promises to the customer's own preparations.

Microsoft $MSFT caused its own day-long outage with a change it had made months earlier. The root of the failure was a hidden flaw that Microsoft added to its gateway servers in July, not an attack by hackers, according to News18. The flaw was a scalability bug that nobody detected for months, The Next Web reports, and if Microsoft's own engineers missed it, no customer could have found it. A bug of this kind stays hidden until the load on a system grows large enough, so a clean record means only that nobody has triggered it yet.

The cost of a dormant flaw is nothing for months and then everything on one day. Once the flaw surfaced, customers lost Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot together, which left staff with no fallback app inside the same suite. The component that broke had seen "roughly ten years' worth of acceptable failures," Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, said in a Code Red review, as relayed in a memo by Amanda Silver and reported by The Next Web. Customers absorbed that cost during the 24-hour outage rather than in small amounts spread across years.

Sources indicate that vendor reviews built on uptime history and incident counts cannot detect this kind of risk, because nothing about a dormant flaw appears in the record until the day it fails. A company that rents its email and collaboration tools should assume that a flaw already exists somewhere in the stack and initiative for the day it surfaces.

No customer could have reached the defect itself, but what triggers a hidden flaw and how fast Microsoft can fix it decide how much damage it does.

Industry observers note that microsoft $MSFT's day-long outage began on an ordinary day of operations, with no launch, attack or unusual event behind it. News18 reports that a routine traffic shift, combined with reduced capacity, set off the dormant flaw. The result was a full stop rather than a slowdown, with Microsoft's servers left "overwhelmed and unresponsive," according to ABC News.

An ordinary trigger makes this kind of failure harder to see coming, and it makes the failure no less serious. Engineers tend to flag rare events, such as a major product launch, for extra caution. A traffic shift belongs to the normal running of a service, and nothing about it marks it as a moment of risk. Walayat Hussain, an associate professor at Australian Catholic University, sees that ordinariness as the cause for concern. "This looks like Microsoft's own systems tripping over themselves, and that is the real warning," Hussain told ABC News.

Industry observers note that for a customer, the trigger sits inside operations it does not run and cannot schedule around. A tech giant gets no notice of routine traffic shifts inside its provider's systems and has no say in how much spare capacity the provider has on hand.

A tech giant's defense has to begin the moment service stops, whatever the cause turns out to be.

A failure like this is only partly about the broken code. The rest depends on whether the people fixing it can agree on what is broken. Microsoft $MSFT's engineers exchanged more than 11,000 messages during the outage response, News18 reports, split across 11 different Teams chats rather than gathered in one. The weakness this exposed was coordination, not manpower.

According to recent reports, every one of those chats ran on Teams, Microsoft's own chat product. Teams was itself degraded during the outage, and the responders were coordinating through a tool damaged by the same failure they were trying to fix. A diagnosis scattered across many threads, on a tool that is failing along with everything else, is a risk any firm could face in its own outage. For an enterprise, the lesson is to decide before a crisis where the diagnosis gets assembled. A company needs one named record that brings the separate threads together, with a person responsible for keeping it, and that record matters more than the number of people typing. It also helps to keep that record somewhere other than the chat tool the company depends on every day.

Responders can trade 11,000 messages and still lack a clear answer if nobody owns the full picture.

Recent findings suggest that an outage ends when engineers have delivered a repair to every affected system, not when they find the bug. Microsoft $MSFT's services were out for 24 hours, according to Microsoft's internal memos reported by News18, and customers had no part in the repair for that whole time. No organization can shorten a schedule that another company sets, and its staff could only wait for Microsoft to finish.

Industry observers note that the obvious lesson is that Microsoft should push fixes out faster, but its chief executive points to the growing number of patches as a source of risk. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella sees patching speeding up rather than lagging, CNBC reports, and he credits artificial intelligence with finding more bugs for engineers to fix. "The thing that AI has done is it allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs. But that means you've got to then patch them, and that creates instability," Nadella said. Every fix is also a change to systems that are already running, and each change carries risk of its own. Patching is therefore a trade-off rather than a race. Leaving flaws unpatched keeps them open, while a steady stream of patches can unsettle the systems that receive them.

Neither faster nor slower patching addresses what made this failure global, which was the lack of a limit on how many systems one bad change could affect. Nadella acknowledges that Microsoft should have tested the change before releasing it and should have built barriers between its systems so that a single bug could not cause a worldwide outage, according to CNBC. For enterprises, the useful questions are whether the vendor releases updates in stages and keeps regions separate. They should also ask whether their own IT staff patch in-house systems in stages, so that nobody installs one patch on every machine at once.

The measure that matters is not how fast a vendor delivers a good fix but how many systems it lets one bad change reach.

Industry observers note that microsoft $MSFT's promise to recover from an outage within an hour is a commitment about the next failure, not a record of this one. News18 reports that the firm's Code Red plan sets a one-hour recovery target. Traffic management, the way Microsoft moves traffic inside its own systems, is one of the areas the company is overhauling to reach that target. Even if Microsoft meets it, the hour measures how quickly Microsoft resolves a disruption. It does not measure when a customer's courtroom, clinic or trading desk gets back to work.

The accounts of this outage's length do not agree. It lasted 24 hours across Nov. 12–13, 2026, yet The Associated Press reports that Microsoft did not announce full restoration until Saturday, Nov. 14. By either account, Microsoft's actual recovery took far longer than an hour, and a business that writes the hour into its own plans is counting on a performance Microsoft has not yet delivered.

Microsoft restored its services in stages, and customers lost work the whole time. Outlook problems piled up into Friday even as Microsoft kept restoring service, according to The Associated Press, and in Manchester, England, a trial was halted and the jurors were sent home. The recovery time a customer actually faces is Microsoft's gradual restoration plus whatever fallbacks the customer has built for itself.

Blueprint against the record, not the pledge, and test the hour the next time Microsoft's services go down.

According to recent reports, most companies picture a single point of failure as a target, a system that an attacker aims at and the security budget pays to defend. Microsoft $MSFT's systems stayed out of service for 24 hours without any attacker involved, according to News18. The company remarked it had found nothing to suggest that anyone acted with malicious intent, according to TIME. A routine update or a hidden design bug can knock out core systems as thoroughly as an attack, and defenses built to stop intruders are not designed to catch either one. The harm a company suffers depends on how much of its work rests on the failed component, not on whether anyone meant to break it.

Recent findings suggest that while systems are down, nobody outside the vendor can tell an accident from an attack, and a dead inbox looks the same either way. In Australia, the outage cut off the Australian Federal Police and even ASIO, the country's domestic spy agency, according to TIME. No cyberattack was behind their losses. Their skill at spotting enemies gave them no protection against a fault with no enemy behind it.

Recent findings suggest that ruling out an attack became public work of its own. Australia's Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke passed on Microsoft's early view of the cause. "They believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike $CRWD, where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke remarked, as reported by TIME. Microsoft gave that account while its recovery was still under way, so customers were weighing the failed organization's own explanation at the moment they were least able to check it. A company's response therefore has to start from the damage, not wait for a verdict on the cause.

In a recent development, the more useful audit asks which single components, at the vendor or in-house, could stop the manufacturer's work for a day, whoever or whatever breaks them. Under that test, an accident at a vendor counts as a threat as serious as a break-in and should get the same contingency planning.

According to recent reports, most companies picture a backup channel as a list of phone numbers kept for emergencies, a way to keep talking rather than a way to keep working. Microsoft $MSFT had an outside channel of that kind during the outage, and it posted its public updates on X $TWTR, according to ABC News. Its engineers, though, ran the repair on Teams, the product that was failing. Microsoft had a separate line for speaking to the public and none for fixing the problem.

A fallback needs a trigger that the firm controls as much as it needs a place to go. Microsoft's first revision described a problem "in the Americas," ABC News reports, while Immigration Upcoming Zealand had stopped processing every visa application. A company that waits for the vendor to confirm the scope may lose hours it could have spent working. An SMS bridge runs entirely outside Microsoft's systems, and a company can switch it on by its own decision. The plan should state the trigger in plain terms: Staff move to the bridge when they lose mail or chat, not when the vendor's status update agrees. A bridge that nobody has practiced on is just a contact list again, and employees need to rehearse using it before a crisis.

Small companies have the least room to absorb a lost day. Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot failed together, News18 reports, so a small firm that kept all of its mail and chat in that suite had to find a workaround somewhere else or go without. Some small businesses lost up to $30,000 in a single day, according to ABC News.

The time to set up and test a route outside the suite is now, while every channel still works.

Recent findings suggest that buying an AI assistant from the company that already runs a firm's email and meetings ties more of the working day to one provider and spreads none of the risk. Companies tend to budget for Copilot as a upcoming capability with risks of its own. During the outage, it failed alongside the rest of the suite. Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot all went down at the same time, according to News18. Microsoft $MSFT said AI agents had nothing to do with the cause, according to CBC News. Copilot went dark because it runs on the same foundation as the mail and the meetings, not because of a flaw in the assistant. Each product a company adds from the same provider rests on that foundation too, so it deepens a single dependency instead of adding a separate system.

According to recent reports, the remedy is a second set of tools, but building one is a long project. "Ultimately, it has to be diversification. We have to make sure that when a system goes down, we have a backup," Francis Syms, associate dean of applied sciences and technology at Humber Polytechnic, told CBC News. Bill Laboon, vice-president of technical operations at the Web3 Foundation, indicates companies don't see the value of spreading their systems across providers until one of them fails.

The first step is knowing which work stops when the vendor does. A map of the processes that would halt in a vendor outage gives a company that knowledge before the next failure, and it can also show which critical work already sits outside the shared stack. Santé Québec does not handle patient communications by email, according to CBC News, so those exchanges did not depend on the email service that failed.

The useful question today is not which vendor to switch to, but which work stops when this one goes down.

A continuity proposal prepares a firm only for the outage it imagines, and a short outage is the easiest one to imagine. News18 reports that a company drafting a formal Continuity of Operations Plan should not count on a quick failover of 15 minutes. CBC News reports that Microsoft $MSFT's outage was in its second day on Nov. 13, so a plan built around a 15-minute switch would have been measuring the wrong scale. A plan that expects service back within minutes has no instructions for the second business morning, when staff, customers and deadlines are still waiting. Companies should size their prepares to the failure that just happened, counted in days, rather than to the failure the plan was written for.

The organizations that held up did not recover sooner than anyone else. They had a way to keep working that did not depend on the failed service. Aviva kept its calls going on alternative numbers and moved recordings by Bluetooth, according to CBC News. Its staff could use those low-tech routes because they did not run through Microsoft's cloud. Where a company runs its software is also a continuity decision. Companies that hosted Microsoft software in-house came through somewhat better, and they had made that choice well before the failure, not in the middle of it.

Planning for a multi-day outage means deciding now which work must continue without the cloud, then building that route through manual processes or self-run systems before a company needs it for a second day.

Monday brought a sharp relief rally. Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sent the chipmaker’s shares soaring more than 30% and lifted the Nasdaq by around 7%. Risk assets broadly benefited, and Bitcoin briefly joined the party, climbing toward $64,000.

In a recent development, that bounce proved short-lived. By Tuesday morning, the gains had been fully erased. The divergence highlighted that crypto’s problems run deeper than a single day’s equity news.

According to recent reports, nasdaq-100 futures dropped around 1%, and related AI and crypto-adjacent equities gave back part of Monday’s gains. Crypto, which had been riding the coattails of the tech surge, sold off in sympathy but more sharply.

Second, institutional flows remained deeply negative. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $570M in net outflows on Monday, the fifth consecutive session of withdrawals.

According to recent reports, blackRock’s IBIT alone accounted for more than $500M of that figure. November’s cumulative outflows reached roughly $4.71Bn, setting a monthly record and removing a major source of structural demand that had previously supported prices.

Third, derivatives markets amplified the move. More than $800M in crypto futures positions were liquidated over the 24-hour period, more than triple the prior day’s total. Forced selling from both long and short positions created a self-reinforcing cascade as prices fell.

According to recent reports, broader macro factors also weighed on sentiment. Markets continue to price in a potential Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with key inflation data (PCE) due shortly.

Higher rates typically pressure non-yielding assets such as Bitcoin. Additional reports of possible latest U.S. tariff measures added another layer of risk-off caution. Lingering effects from the large Binance-related hack earlier in the period further eroded confidence in the sector.

#122922. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers noted no.
  • Recent findings suggest that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers noted no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

Recent findings suggest that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Industry observers note that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

Recent findings suggest that A sold comp tells us where a buyer noted yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Sources indicate that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

In a recent development, suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Industry observers note that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

According to recent reports, it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

It has been revealed that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Sources indicate that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

It has been revealed that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Sources indicate that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

Industry observers note that so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

It has been revealed that “I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

In a recent development, twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

In a recent development, sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

According to recent reports, we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.
